ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: d=0.23 is now smaller than the d=-0.36 used in power analysis — must cross-reference
ground_truth.original_snippet: In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.23, 0.86], regarded as a medium effect similar to Study 1.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.01, 0.45], regarded as a small effect.
ground_truth.description: Changed Study 3 d from 0.55 to 0.23 — makes power analysis based on d=-0.36 no longer the most conservative estimate; study may be underpowered for this smaller effect

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Within-subjects impossible for learning manipulation; df in ANOVA tables inconsistent
ground_truth.original_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single between-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.description: Changed between-subjects to within-subjects — impossible for this intervention (learning about IVE permanently changes cognition); df in ANOVA tables are inconsistent with within-subjects

matched_finding.subcategory: within-subject design inconsistent with condition cell counts
matched_finding.description: The manuscript describes the design as within-subject, but the tables show separate between-subject cell sizes summing to N=1000 across six cells. A within-subject design would require each participant to provide responses in multiple/all conditions and would require repeated-measures analyses. This ambiguity prevents evaluation of the design and invalidates the reported ANOVAs if the design was truly within-subject.
matched_finding.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Cognitive evaluations measured but paper discusses 'affective feelings' throughout — cross-section mismatch
ground_truth.original_snippet: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different affective reactions they experienced which may influence their choice of donation. These items included the feeling of being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, and the appropriateness of donation to hel...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation. These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds...
ground_truth.description: Replaced affective measures with cognitive evaluations — IVE theory is explicitly affect-driven (affect heuristic); cognitive measures can't test the proposed emotional mechanism

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Self-selection into conditions visible but subtle — 'selected their preferred' reads naturally
ground_truth.original_snippet: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.
ground_truth.description: Replaced random assignment with self-selection — eliminates internal validity; empathetic people may choose identifiable victim condition

matched_finding.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This eliminates random assignment, introduces severe selection bias, and makes causal comparisons between conditions uninterpretable. It also contradicts the experimental framing and original design.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Statistical victims donate MORE contradicts the identifiable victim effect being replicated
ground_truth.original_snippet: meaning that participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.description: Reversed which condition has higher donations — IVE is now reversed (statistical > identifiable), contradicting the phenomenon being replicated and Table 11 descriptives

matched_finding.subcategory: incorrect or inconsistent direction of reported post-hoc effect
matched_finding.description: The table reports Identifiable vs Statistical t = -2.40, but the narrative states statistical victims had higher donation. The descriptive table actually implies the identifiable mean across intervention/no-intervention cells is approximately 2.54 and statistical approximately 2.24, the opposite of the narrative. This suggests reversed labels, arithmetic error, or incorrect interpretation.
matched_finding.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Power analysis details absent — must independently expect specific parameters for a replication

Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention (learning identifiable victim effect or not) on donation was found in the original stud...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of "Power analysis of the original study effect".
ground_truth.description: Removed specific power parameters (power=.95, alpha=.05, d=-.36, N=314) — reader cannot evaluate power adequacy or whether target effect size is appropriate

matched_finding.subcategory: power analysis details missing from manuscript
matched_finding.description: The manuscript refers readers to supplementary materials for the power analysis but does not report the target effect size, alpha, desired power, allocation assumptions, exclusions, or achieved detectable effect. This prevents evaluation of whether N=1000 is justified, especially for interactions and condition-specific contrasts.
matched_finding.quote: The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Says 'no exclusion' then lists exclusions — direct contradiction
ground_truth.original_snippet: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.
ground_truth.description: Added non-preregistered exclusions — prior-knowledge exclusion biases toward IVE-naive participants; contradicts 'no exclusion' claim earlier

matched_finding.description: The manuscript states participants with prior knowledge or failed attention checks were excluded but does not report how many were excluded, whether exclusions were preregistered, whether N=1000 is before or after exclusions, or exclusion criteria wording.
matched_finding.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Availability vs affect heuristic — must know these are different mechanisms with different predictions
ground_truth.original_snippet: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The automatic "affect heuristic"  (Slovic, Finucane, Peters, & MacGregor, 2007), which relies on emotional arousal for decision making, is believed to be activa...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The "availability heuristic"  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated whe...
ground_truth.description: Replaced affect heuristic (emotional arousal) with availability heuristic (memory retrieval) — changes the theoretical mechanism; intervention design and feeling measures no longer match the theory

matched_finding.description: The manuscript attributes stronger responses to identifiable victims to the availability heuristic, but the explanation given is more about vividness, affect, concreteness, and sympathy than availability as frequency/probability judgment based on retrieval ease. This conceptual imprecision weakens the theoretical framing.
matched_finding.quote: The “availability heuristic”... is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual... The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress
